items.title: William James identified four marks of mystical experience
items.claim: What are James's four marks of mystical experience?

options.text: Ineffability (cannot be fully described), noetic quality (provides knowledge), transiency (does not last long), passivity (the subject feels acted upon) — set out in 'The Varieties of Religious Experience' (1902)

items.reveal:
James's Gifford Lectures (1901-02) became 'The Varieties of Religious Experience'. He aimed to study religion empirically as a phenomenon of consciousness, regardless of any metaphysical truth claims.

His four marks were intended as descriptive criteria, not arguments for divine reality. Richard Swinburne ('The Existence of God', 1979) and others later used religious experience evidentially — the principle of credulity (we should believe perceptions unless we have reason not to) and the principle of testimony.

Critics including Walter Kaufmann and Steven Katz have argued that mystical experience is heavily shaped by prior cultural framework — a Buddhist's experience is structured by Buddhist concepts.
items.why: Religious experience is studied both descriptively (what do people report?) and evaluatively (what does it prove?). James's framework remains the starting point for both — a century of subsequent debate has built on his typology.

items.title: Moral and natural evil are distinct problems for theism
items.claim: What is the distinction between moral and natural evil?

options.text: All evil is caused by human moral failure

Moral evil is caused by free moral agents (murder, torture, cruelty); natural evil is caused by impersonal natural processes (earthquakes, disease, predation) — they raise different problems for theistic theodicies
Natural evil is just a subset of moral evil

items.reveal:
Free Will Defence (Augustine, Alvin Plantinga) explains moral evil as the cost of human free will — but doesn't obviously address natural evil. Earthquakes do not flow from human choices.

Irenaean theodicy (revived by John Hick, 'Evil and the God of Love', 1966) sees natural evil as part of soul-making — character development requires a challenging environment.

Augustinian theodicy treats evil as privatio boni (privation of good) — not a substance but an absence. The Fall extends moral consequences into nature.

The logical problem of evil (J. L. Mackie, 'Evil and Omnipotence', 1955) has been largely answered by Plantinga's free-will defence; the evidential problem (William Rowe, 1979) remains live.
items.why: The problem of evil is the most persistent challenge to classical theism. The moral/natural and logical/evidential distinctions shape which theodicies are even relevant — generic answers miss the structure of the argument.
